Lambert Daneau
läm-bĕr´ dä-nō´
n. (Lambert Daneau, c. 1530–1595, French Reformed pastor and theologian, Beza's colleague at Geneva and professor at Leiden, author of the first Reformed system of Christian ethics)
French Daneau, Latinized Danaeus; Lambert, from Germanic Landberht, land-bright.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Lambert Daneau was converted by the death of Anne du Bourg, a councillor burned at Paris in 1559, studied under Calvin and Beza, pastored in France through the wars, and taught at Geneva and then as the first professor of theology at Leiden. His Ethices Christianae of 1577 is the first full Reformed system of Christian ethics, and its method is the lasting contribution: it organizes the moral life under the Decalogue, treats the law as the believer's rule and not his righteousness, and derives duties from Scripture rather than from Aristotle's virtues. Mic 6:8 is its governing question — “what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?” Tit 2:12 gives grace itself as the teacher, “Teaching us that, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we should live soberly, righteously, and godly, in this present world.” Rom 12:2 forbids conformity to the world, and Psa 119:11 names the means: “Thy word have I hid in mine heart, that I might not sin against thee.”

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines ethics as the doctrine of morals; a system of moral principles; the science of moral philosophy, which teaches men their duty and the reasons of it.

expand to see more

ETH'ICS, n. The doctrine of morals; a system of moral principles; a system of rules for regulating the actions and manners of men in society.

ETH'ICAL, a. Relating to morals or manners; treating of morality; delivering precepts of morality.

MORAL'ITY, n. The doctrine or system of moral duties, or the duties of men in their social character.

Key Scripture

Mic 6:8 — "He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?"

Tit 2:12 — "Teaching us that, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we should live soberly, righteously, and godly, in this present world;"

Rom 12:2 — "And be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind, that ye may prove what is that good, and acceptable, and perfect, will of God."

Psa 119:11 — "Thy word have I hid in mine heart, that I might not sin against thee."

Modern Corruption

Daneau built Christian ethics on the Decalogue under grace, which is the only arrangement that is neither legalism nor the loss of the law.

expand to see more

Two errors stand on either side of Daneau's method. The first is legalism, which makes obedience the ground of acceptance; the Reformed answer is that the believer is justified by faith alone and the law is thereafter his rule, not his righteousness. The second is antinomianism, which concludes from justification that the law has no further claim; Tit 2:12 forecloses it by making grace itself the teacher of sober and righteous living. Daneau's arrangement — the Decalogue as the structure of Christian duty, within a covenant of grace — is the one the Heidelberg Catechism and the Westminster Larger follow, and it is the standing Reformed shape of ethics.

The nearer corruption is the modern substitution of principles for commandments. Christian ethics is now commonly taught as the application of broad values — love, justice, flourishing — to cases, which sounds generous and in practice lets the culture supply the content of each term. Mic 6:8 is often quoted in that service, with the third clause quietly dropped; the verse requires walking humbly with God, which anchors justice and mercy to His revealed will. The recovery is Daneau's: ten commandments, expounded, applied, and preached to the justified.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek eusebeia, godliness; suschematizo (G4964), to conform to a pattern; Hebrew tsana (H6800), to be humble.

Hebrew mishpat (H4941) — judgment, justice; Micah 6:8.

Hebrew tsana (H6800) — to be lowly, to walk humbly; Micah 6:8.

Greek paideuo (G3811) — to train, to teach by discipline; Titus 2:12.

Greek suschematizo (G4964) — to conform to a pattern; Romans 12:2.

Hebrew tsaphan (H6845) — to hide, to treasure up; Psalm 119:11.

Usage

"“what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?” (Mic 6:8) — his governing question."

"“denying ungodliness and worldly lusts” (Tit 2:12) — grace as the teacher."

"“Thy word have I hid in mine heart, that I might not sin against thee” (Psa 119:11) — the means."
